title: Check a subfloor for large-format tile with a straightedge and a measuring wedge, then tag it PASS or FAIL
instruction: Check whether this subfloor is flat enough for large-format tile, along the strip between the two pencil lines. Leave the measuring wedge in the deepest gap under the straightedge, and put the tag puck in PASS or FAIL.
context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031.00; about 959,000 US jobs in 2024, BLS) build and prepare subfloors, and O*NET lists "Verify trueness of structure, using plumb bob and level." as a core task; tile setters make the same check before large-format tile goes down. A straightedge stands on its edge on the floor's high points and a tapered measuring wedge slides into the gap under it until it stops; its scale there gives the gap. ANSI A108.02 allows 1/16 in (1.6 mm) in 24 in, measured from the high points, for tile with any edge 15 in or longer; past that the tile bridges the low spot, which leaves hollows that crack. The trough can't be seen, so the check has to find the deepest place, and the wedge has to go in gently: pushed hard, it lifts the straightedge and reads high.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z 0. (1) Subfloor section, fixed: 3/4 in (1.9 cm) panel, 23 cm deep (x 22 to 45) by 64 cm long (y -32 to 32), plywood face. Two pencil lines across it at x 32 and x 38, 6 cm apart, mark the check line. A sag between joists crosses the line as a trough: the floor is made of 2 cm strips along y; on each case's board the three middle strips (6 cm) sit lower by the trough's depth, and each strip further out is 0.5 mm less deep. Cases (depth, center of the deepest strip): 1: 1.0 mm at y -13; 2: 1.5 mm at y 7; 3: 2.0 mm at y -5; 4: 2.5 mm at y 15; 5: 3.0 mm at y -3; 6: 1.5 mm at y -9; 7: 2.0 mm at y 11; 8: 1.0 mm at y 3. Cases 1, 2, 6 and 8 are within 1.6 mm (PASS); 3, 4, 5 and 7 are not (FAIL). The trough cannot be seen by eye or by the cameras. (2) Straightedge: a 24 in aluminum box-beam level used on its milled bottom edge, 61.0 cm long, 2.5 cm thick, 6.3 cm tall, 0.50 kg, standing on its edge along y in two fixed rubber rests at x 19, y -20 and y 20 (rest top 3 cm up, a 2.7 cm slot between 1.5 cm cheeks). (3) Measuring wedge: aluminum, 15 cm long, 3.0 cm wide, 0.3 mm thick at the tip rising 1:10 to 15.3 mm at the heel, 95 g, with a mark every 0.5 mm of reading (5 mm apart along it), longer every 1 mm. It lies flat on the table at x 19.5 to 34.5, y -39, tip pointing away from the robot. (4) Report board, fixed: white plate 18 x 8 cm at x 27, y 39, with two pockets 5.0 cm square inside, 1 cm deep, 5 mm walls: PASS (green, check mark) centered at x 32.5, y 38 and FAIL (red, X) at x 21.5, y 38. (5) Tag puck: white-anodized aluminum, 3.2 cm across, 2.0 cm tall, 43 g, standing on a ring between the pockets at x 27, y 38. Each run draws its case at random, all eight equally likely (FLATNESS_CASE in the README fixes it); everything else is the same in every case.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial; each level must hold for the last 1 s. Contact means two rigid faces within 0.5 mm (the simulator's resting gap). The straightedge is set when it stands on its edge (within 5 degrees), its whole bottom lies between the pencil lines, some point of its bottom touches the floor within each end's last 5 cm (so it rests on the high points), and it is still. The wedge is in a gap when at least 2 mm of it is under the straightedge's near bottom edge, it lies flat (within 3 degrees) pointing under the edge (within 20 degrees of square), its top touches the edge and its bottom the floor there, and it is still. Its reading is the scale at that edge: 0.3 mm + 0.1 x the length of wedge under it. Still means under 5 mm/s and 6 degrees/s. The trial scores 1.0 when the straightedge is set, the wedge is in a gap with a reading within 0.3 mm of the trough's depth and its whole 3 cm width on the deepest 6 cm, and the tag puck stands upright (within 15 degrees) at rest in the correct pocket: PASS if the depth is 1.6 mm or less, FAIL if more. It scores 0.75 when all of that holds but the puck is not in a pocket, 0.5 when the wedge is in a gap but not reading the deepest place (a measurement was made), and 0.25 when only the straightedge is set (the reference every reading needs). Otherwise it scores 0, including when nothing is done. The score is capped at 0.5 when a gripper still touches the straightedge, wedge or puck at the end (the check isn't finished while a hand holds a tool on the floor), when the puck is in the wrong pocket (a wrong report sends tile onto a bad floor or a crew to fix a good one), or when the puck reached a pocket before the wedge first measured a gap under the set straightedge (a guess; remembered for the whole trial). Why 0.3 mm: the next strip out is 0.5 mm shallower, so a reading there misses by 0.5 mm; the wedge must also lie on the deepest 6 cm, so a wedge forced in on the next strip can't pass by lifting an end inside the contact allowance. Arm position is not scored. Real trial (one test board per case, depth known): check both straightedge ends with the 0.5 mm feeler, tape the wedge's centerline (within 1.5 cm of the deepest window's center), and photograph the scale at the edge and the pocket from above.
reset_notes: Put in the board for the trial's case (one board per case; nothing is used up). Stand the straightedge back in its rests, lay the wedge in its place on the table and the puck on its ring.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at real size and mass (PhysX). The trough is 2 cm strips in 0.5 mm steps, as in the real test boards. The scorer computes the wedge's reading from the wedge's and the straightedge's poses where the edge crosses the scale; a real trial reads the scale on a photo.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (board case 5, 2,400 steps); demo: 1.0 (board case 2, 1,091 steps; case 3, 1,141 steps)
